It took America seventy years to say thank you properly. In 2013, it finally did. 🇺🇸

The Navajo were honored first, in 2001 — but they were never the only ones. Choctaw and Cherokee soldiers had spoken the first coded words in 1918. Comanche men hit Utah Beach on D-Day. Twenty-seven Meskwaki from one small Iowa tribe served together in North Africa. Hopi, Lakota, Pawnee, Creek, Seminole and more — in all, members of more than thirty tribes carried their languages into America's wars, and most of them went to their graves officially unrecognized.

The Code Talkers Recognition Act of 2008 set out to fix that, and on November 20, 2013, in the United States Capitol, it happened: Congressional Gold Medals were presented honoring twenty-five more tribes' code talkers, with silver medals for the individual men and their families. Old soldiers in red caps and yellow scarves — and widows and grandsons standing in for those who never lived to see it — finally heard a grateful nation say their names out loud.

The men in this photograph, Navajo elders in their eighties and nineties, sat for honors that arrived two generations late. Their verdict on the long wait was the same grace they'd shown in 1945: no bitterness, just pride. The medals were gold. The men were better.

For twenty-three years, America's greatest battlefield secret was guarded by the men's own silence. 🇺🇸

When the code talkers came home in 1945, their officers gave them one final order: tell no one. Not their wives, not their children, not anyone — what they had done, and how. The code was still a classified military asset, and so some of America's most remarkable veterans went back to their farms, ranches and oil fields carrying a story they were forbidden to share.

They kept that silence until 1968, when the Pentagon finally declassified the code talker program. Only then — twenty-three years later — could the men explain the strange questions their families had always wondered about. Slowly, the nation began to understand: President Reagan proclaimed a National Navajo Code Talkers Day in 1982; in 2001, the surviving Original 29 received Congressional Gold Medals, and every other Navajo talker the Silver.

The men in this photograph are the elders of that brotherhood in their later years, gathered at their traveling display — the portraits of their fallen friends on the banner behind them — still driving to schools, museums and veterans' events in their nineties to tell the story in person. Every year, there are fewer chairs filled at that table. What they ask of us is simple: remember the code, and remember who spoke it.

On the night of January 23, 2002, Master Sergeant Anthony Pryor led his Special Forces team through a night assault on a suspected Taliban hideout. The Green Berets met heavy fire but attacked through it into the compound. Pryor and another soldier were clearing a building room by room when they accidentally became separated during a firefight. Pryor killed one insurgent before entering a room by himself, where he found and killed two more insurgents firing out a window. As Pryor changed magazines, another insurgent behind him smashed a board down on his back, breaking his clavicle and dislocating his shoulder. The man jumped him ripped off Pryor's night vision goggles, and began pushing his fingers into Pryor's eyes. Pryor flipped the man over, and they both landed on the floor. The impact popped his shoulder back into place. Pryor now faced the man eye-to-eye, both of them weaponless.

Seventeen men. One language. Zero messages broken. 🇺🇸

This is the full team: the Comanche code talkers of the U.S. Army's 4th Signal Company, 4th Infantry Division — front row, second from right, Charles Chibitty; with him Roderick Red Elk, Simmons Parker, Larry Saupitty, Melvin Permansu, Willie Yackeshi, Wellington Mihecoby, and behind them Morris Sunrise, Perry Noyebad, Ralph Wahnee, Haddon Codynah, Robert Holder, Albert Nahquaddy, Clifford Ototivo and Forrest Tsimpoid, among their brothers of the seventeen.

Recruited from Oklahoma beginning in 1940 and hardened at Fort Benning, Georgia, these men built a Comanche military vocabulary of more than a hundred terms — because their ancient language had no words for things like tanks, bombers or Adolf Hitler, they invented them: Hitler became "Crazy White Man," a tank a "turtle," and a machine gun a "sewing machine." Then they memorized all of it, because in the field, nothing could be written.

On D-Day they hit Utah Beach with the first waves of the 4th Infantry Division and kept the division talking — securely — from Normandy to the heart of Germany. Not one Comanche transmission was ever understood by the enemy. Seventeen men did that. When the Army finally told the story decades later, America learned that one of its most effective secret weapons in Europe had been a language spoken around Comanche campfires for a thousand years.

Todd Corbin - Navy Cross Recipient in the face of danger, most would run toward safety. Yet, when then-Lance Cpl. Corbin was faced with such a decision, he ran toward peril and possible death – braving intense enemy fire to help injured comrades.

Corbin, a medium tactical vehicle replacement driver, and his unit were stationed in the Al Anbar province to help secure and stabilize the volatile area. They had just finished several days of routine patrol on May 7, 2005, and were returning to the Haditha Dam when they got the call.

A platoon from their battalion was under attack on the east side of the Euphrates River and needed support to block the insurgents' retreat. Corbin's team – a quick reaction force (QRF) – quickly responded to the call. As the QRF crept toward the attack site, there was an unnatural stillness in the air.

“There was no one out, nothing moving,” Corbin later told the Marine Corps Times.

With every nerve on alert, the QRF kept driving toward the ambush site, knowing there were injured Marines that needed them. Suddenly, a vehicle laden with IEDs sped toward the convoy and blew up between two of the Humvees. Another blast followed as enemy fighters began firing upon the group.

The swift attack devastated Corbin's team – three of the four vehicles were severely damaged, and 11 of 16 Marines were injured or killed. Taking control of the situation, Corbin immediately repositioned his vehicle between the insurgents' fire and the wounded Marines. As he radioed in the situation, he began directing a counter-attack.

As those that could returned fire, Corbin began recovering dead and wounded personnel and moving them toward safety. Running through the line of fire, Corbin grabbed his wounded patrol leader and threw him over his shoulder. He then sprinted back to his Humvee, firing at enemies as he ran. Corbin ran back and forth several times through the kill zone, moving everyone he could out of the withering fire and loaded them into his vehicle.

Arming every able Marine with as much ammunition and weapons as they could hold, Corbin drove his severely damaged Humvee through the kill zone toward the battle aid station. Even injured, the Marines were a deadly force to be reckoned with. Insurgents continued to pelt the rumbling truck with mortars and small-arms fire, but the Marines made it to safety.

Corbin's quick actions ensured that no Marines were killed after that initial attack. For his leadership, Corbin was awarded the Navy Cross on April 12, 2006.

Charles Joyce Chibitty was a Comanche kid from near Medicine Park, Oklahoma, when the Army came looking for men who spoke his language. He became one of just seventeen Comanche code talkers assigned to the 4th Infantry Division — a tiny band of men carrying an outsized secret into the biggest invasion in history.

On the morning of June 6, 1944, Chibitty came ashore at Utah Beach on D-Day, among the very first code talkers to put the language to work in Europe. From that beachhead across France and into Germany, the Comanche talkers sent their coded messages — tank became "turtle," a bomber a "pregnant airplane," a machine gun a "sewing machine" — and German intelligence, for all its brilliance, never understood a single transmission.

Chibitty fought through the whole campaign and came home to Oklahoma, where in his later years he became the honored elder of the Comanche code talkers — traveling, teaching, and reminding America that Native men had helped win the war in a voice straight from their own grandmothers' kitchens. Honors found him at last, including the Army's Knowlton Award for intelligence work. When Charles Chibitty died on July 20, 2005, the last surviving Comanche code talker went silent — but the seventeen voices of the 4th Signal Company are part of D-Day forever.

The code talkers did not begin in World War II. They began in France, in 1918. 🇺🇸

In October 1918, during the Meuse-Argonne offensive, the American 36th Division had a deadly problem: German listeners tapped their phone lines at will, and every code the Americans tried was broken within hours. Then an officer overheard two of his own soldiers chatting in Choctaw — and realized he was listening to a language no German on Earth could understand.

Within days, Choctaw soldiers of the 141st Infantry were manning field telephones across the sector, relaying orders for troop movements and artillery in their native tongue. The Germans were stunned into silence. Within twenty-four hours the tide in the sector turned; within seventy-two, the surprised enemy was in full retreat — and American officers were writing reports calling the Choctaw telephone squad one of the cleverest moves of the war.

Nineteen Choctaw men are remembered as the first code talkers — the pioneers whose idea the Navajo, Comanche and two dozen other tribes would carry into the next war. Yet when they came home, their story was buried for decades; most Americans never learned their names in their lifetimes. It took until 2008 for Congress to formally honor them, and 2013 for their gold medals to be struck. This photograph is where the whole legend starts: a group of young Choctaw soldiers, an American flag, and a language that saved lives.

The Marine Corps is fast-tracking two critical medical capabilities directly to frontline infantry squads: handheld, AI-powered ultrasound scanners and battery-operated whole-blood refrigeration units.

Reporting from Marine Corps Times and Military Times highlights that emerging combat doctrine specifically Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations (EABO) across remote Pacific islands renders the traditional "golden hour" helicopter medevac nearly impossible due to enemy anti-ship and anti-air missile bubbles. With small teams facing prolonged field care scenarios where evacuation could be delayed for days, corpsmen need diagnostic power at the point of injury. The new AI-assisted ultrasound systems guide non-physicians step-by-step to detect internal bleeding and collapsed lungs in seconds, while ruggedized portable coolers keep whole blood viable in austere tropical heat.

In 2004, US Marine 1stSgt. Brad Kasal was engaged in a firefight with insurgents during the Second Battle of Fallujah. He was hit by seven 7.62mm rounds and 47 pieces of shrapnel from a fragmentation grenade. While fighting, he used his body to shield another Marine. He was responsible for saving the lives of several Marines under his command. After being taken out of the house by his Marines, he was still holding his M9 Beretta pistol and his Ka-Bar knife. He refused to lie on a litter to deny the enemy the satisfaction of seeing him in a supine position. After arriving at the field hospital, it was determined that he had lost 60% of his blood. It was later determined that he had over 100 puncture wounds. As a result of his injuries, he lost four inches of bone in his right leg. He has undergone 21 surgeries to repair the injuries to his leg. For his actions, he was awarded several medals, including the Navy Cross for valor. He retired in 2018 from the Marine Corps at the rank of Sgt. Major.

The U.S. Army has dispatched maintenance teams to remediate living quarters at Camp Hovey, South Korea, after an anonymous soldier publicly exposed severe mold infestations and deteriorating conditions, according to reporting from Stars and Stripes via The American Legion.

The complaintb posted to the military housing review platform Hots&Cots detailed substandard living conditions affecting rotational troops from 1st Squadron, 3rd Cavalry Regiment in Building 3535, situated approximately 15 miles from the Demilitarized Zone. Photos showed black mold spreading across shower floors, peeling bathroom ceilings, and soiled bedding. According to the whistleblower, junior enlisted troops were falling ill while chain-of-command responses were dismissed with instructions to "spray it with a spray."

Following the public post, Col. Chris Choi, commander of U.S. Army Garrison Yongsan-Casey, and 2nd Infantry Division spokesman Lt. Col. Arturo Rodriguez confirmed that installation leaders personally inspected the facility, directing the Directorate of Public Works to expedite repairs and review ventilation systems.

The incident reflects broader systemic maintenance backlogs identified across service branches by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), prompting advocates to alert Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer following his recent appointment as a senior adviser to the Pentagon's barracks task force.

Second Lieutenant Michael Seely guided his battered and flaming AAV out of harms way after an RPG severely damaged the vehicle. Once behind cover, Seely was able to successfully evacuate 4 wounded Marines from the back. Suddenly, a friendly A-10 Warthog began strafing the Marines’ position by mistake. Seely marked their position then sprinted through the area where the aircraft was actively firing to reach a radio and halt the strafing runs. His quick actions directly prevented more Marines from being wounded or killed.

In November 1943, the 2nd Marine Division stormed Betio Island at Tarawa in one of the bloodiest battles in Marine Corps history — more than a thousand Marines lost in just seventy-six hours. In the middle of that chaos, crouched in the rubble with a field telephone pressed to his ear, sat a Navajo code talker, passing the words that kept the battle connected.

Radios failed at Tarawa. Wires were cut, sets drowned in the lagoon, headquarters lost contact with men pinned at the seawall. What could not fail was the code talkers' network: a human chain of voices speaking a language that no amount of enemy listening could unlock. Through them, commanders called down naval gunfire, redirected reserves, and learned where their men still held on.

The young Marine in this photograph has no famous name attached to his picture — and that is exactly the point. The code talkers were not celebrities. They were teenage radiomen who carried the battle's nervous system in their own mouths, island after island, while the world knew nothing about them. Tarawa was their proving ground under the worst conditions imaginable — and the code came through without a single broken message.

THE MEN WHO CAUGHT A DICTATOR: DELTA FORCE OPERATORS ON THE NIGHT OF SADDAM HUSSEIN'S CAPTURE

Posed in front of a modified military vehicle under the cover of night, operators from the U.S. Army's elite 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta (Delta Force) capture a historic moment on December 13, 2003, moments after successfully executing Operation Red Dawn. 

Operation Red Dawn: Operating deep inside a spider hole near a farmhouse in Ad-Dawr, Iraq, Delta Force operators alongside the 4th Infantry Division located and extracted deposed Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein without firing a single shot, ending months of intense manhunts across the country.

The Apex of Tier-1 Direct Action: Known for operating in absolute secrecy, these seasoned operators utilized meticulous intelligence, high-stakes tracking, and lightning-fast assault tactics to dismantle the remnants of the regime's inner circle.

A Definitive Moment in Modern Military History: The capture stands as one of the most famous special operations missions of the Global War on Terrorism, forever etching the quiet professionals of Delta Force into the annals of modern warfare.

The Marines took him at fifteen. The Navajo Nation later made him its leader. 🇺🇸

Peter MacDonald was born in 1928 in Teecnospos, Arizona, raised in a hogan, speaking Navajo — and when he heard the Marines were looking for code talkers, the fifteen-year-old lied about his age and enlisted in 1944. He mastered the secret code, shipped out with the 1st Marine Division, and served in North China as the war ended, one of the youngest men ever to carry America's most guarded battlefield secret in his memory.

Coming home, MacDonald did something just as remarkable: he got an education. He became an electrical engineer — one of the first Navajo engineers in the country — and worked on advanced missile programs before returning to serve his people. In 1970 the Navajo Nation elected him its Chairman, and he would win four terms, the longest-serving leader in the Nation's modern history — a code talker who had defended his country now fighting for his tribe's water, land and future.

Today, in his late nineties, Peter MacDonald remains one of the last living links to the Original Era of the code talkers — a national spokesman who still travels to tell young people what a handful of Navajo voices did in the Pacific. From a fifteen-year-old who lied to serve, to the leader of a nation: his whole life has been one long act of duty.

REMEMBERING GREEN BERET SSG KYU “Q” CHAY: FALLEN AT THE TIP OF THE SPEAR

Today we honor the ultimate sacrifice of Staff Sergeant Kyu “Q” Chay, a veteran Green Beret assigned to the 1st Battalion, 3rd Special Forces Group (Airborne), who gave his life in defense of freedom on October 28, 2006.

From Daegu to the Green Berets: Born in Daegu, South Korea, and raised in New York City, SSG Chay answered the call to serve his adopted country, ultimately earning his Green Beret and deploying into the most demanding operational environments.

At the Tip of the Spear in Afghanistan: Serving as a Special Operations Team-Alpha (SOT-A) assistant team leader, Chay operated in high-threat sectors of southern Afghanistan. On October 28, 2006, at the age of 34, he was killed in the Uruzgan province when an improvised explosive device (IED) detonated near his combat patrol vehicle.

An Enduring Legacy: He left behind a devoted family, including his wife Cathy, son Jason, and daughter Kelly. His sacrifice remains etched into the history of the Green Beret brotherhood and the annals of Operation Enduring Freedom.

Before there were hundreds, there were twenty-nine. 🇺🇸

In May 1942, twenty-nine young Navajo men — shepherds, students, farmers' sons — walked into Marine boot camp as the first all-Navajo platoon in Corps history. At Camp Elliott in San Diego, they were locked into classrooms with a top-secret order: invent an unbreakable code, from scratch, in their own language.

Working day and night, the 29 built it in layers — a phonetic alphabet (A for "ant," B for "bear") and a dictionary of military terms that grew past 400 words, every one of them memorized, because nothing could ever be written down in the field. In testing, they encoded, sent and decoded a three-line message in twenty seconds. The Marines' best machines took thirty minutes.

Their code went to war across the Pacific and was never broken — the only oral code in modern military history that never fell. By 1945 more than 400 Navajo code talkers were serving, and at Iwo Jima their six networks handled more than 800 messages in the first two days without a single error. Their commanding signal officer said it plainly: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."

In 2001, the surviving members of the Original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal. The bronze talker on his knees at Window Rock, radio in hand, stands for all of them — twenty-nine young men who turned the language of home into a shield for a nation.

Remembering the extraordinary courage, quiet professionalism, and ultimate sacrifice of U.S. Army Green Beret Douglas M. Vose III of the 1st Battalion, 10th Special Forces Group (Airborne).  

Service: Born in Roseburg, Oregon, and raised in Concrete, Washington, Vose enlisted in the U.S. Army in April 1989. After spending a decade honing his craft, he earned his Green Beret in 1999 as an 18E Special Forces Communications Sergeant before completing the Warrant Officer Basic Course in 2006. Fluent in German and stationed in Stuttgart, Germany, he served as an Assistant Detachment Commander for Operational Detachment Alpha (ODA) 0114, 1st Battalion, 10th SFG(A). 

On July 29, 2009, while conducting combat operations in Kabul Province, Afghanistan, Vose's element was ambushed with intense, close-range small-arms and RPG fire. With his team pinned down under heavy enemy fire, Vose charged forward to lead from the front and rally his men—an act of selfless valor his commander credited with saving the lives of several teammates before Vose was mortally wounded in the firefight. 

Known by his teammates and family for his relentless work ethic, charisma, and devotion to those he loved, Vose left behind his wife, Nicole, and four children, alongside a permanent legacy of honor within the Special Forces regiment.

He helped invent the only code America ever fielded that was never broken — then he kept it secret for 23 years. 🇺🇸

Chester Nez was a shy teenager from the Navajo Nation when Marine recruiters came looking for men who spoke his language in the spring of 1942. He became one of the Original 29 — the first platoon of Navajo code talkers — the men handed an impossible job: build a battle code out of a language that had almost no written form, and build it in weeks.

They did it. An alphabet. Hundreds of memorized words — "iron fish" for submarine, "hummingbird" for a fighter plane, "turtle" for a tank. Nez then carried that code into some of the fiercest fighting of the Pacific war — Guadalcanal, Bougainville, Guam, Peleliu — sending and receiving orders under fire that Japanese codebreakers could hear perfectly and never once understand.

He came home carrying memories that haunted him for years, and Navajo healing ceremonies helped put the young Marine back in balance. Through it all he said nothing — the code stayed classified until 1968. In 2001 he stood in the Capitol Rotunda as the President placed the Congressional Gold Medal around the original talkers' necks. His memoir, "Code Talker," told the story at last, and when Chester Nez died on June 4, 2014, at 93, the last of the legendary 29 went with him — but the code they built remains unbroken forever.

“It stings but it's nothing.” Most people might say that when describing a carpet burn or perhaps a bee sting. Staff Sgt. Viggiani, on the other hand, said that of a bullet wound sustained on June 3, 2004, in the mountainous region around Khabargho, Afghanistan.

His team and another squad received reports that a group of Taliban fighters were fleeing out of the town and into the forbidding hills – incredibly tough terrain full of caves and crevices, pits, and pitfalls.

As the men approached the ridgeline north of town, Viggiani's squad lost touch with the others as the mountains interfered with the radio transmissions. Then Viggiani and his squad came under heavy and accurate fire, which injured two Marines and halted the advance. Viggiani crept forward, as it seemed like the fire was coming from the steep slope in front of him.
Viggiani and another Marine continued their slow advance – and suddenly came under direct fire. Shooting was coming from a cave just a few feet away, and the enemies were still firing at the wounded Marines who had taken cover behind a nearby rock. With the rest of his team pinned down, it fell to Viggiani to eliminate the well-entrenched insurgents. Maneuvering to a better position, he found himself peering through a small break in the rocks. When he saw a piece of cloth move, he fired off three or four rounds. He heard no sounds that would lead him to believe the enemies had been hit, so he grabbed a grenade and dropped it into the hole. The cave blew apart, exposing three now-dead Taliban snipers.

With the threat eliminated, the medic was able to reach and treat the two injured Marines. Viggiani refused treatment on the gunshot to his leg, and instead continued fighting. After three or four hours of intense chase and fighting, the Marines killed 14 enemy fighters and cleared the area. For his leadership and bravery, Viggiani was awarded the Navy Cross on Jan. 25, 2006.

On this day, October 27, in 1983, U.S. Army Ranger Sergeant Kevin "Doc" Lannon made the ultimate sacrifice during Operation Urgent Fury on the island of Grenada.

A native of Dayton, Ohio, and graduate of Archbishop Alter High School, SGT Lannon served as a combat medic with Headquarters and Headquarters Company (HHC), 2nd Battalion, 75th Infantry (Ranger). On October 25, 1983, he took part in the combat jump onto the Point Salines airfield, helping secure the runway, defending against enemy counterattacks, and rescuing American medical students at the True Blue campus.

According to his Battalion Surgeon, CPT Kane via the US Mountain Ranger Association:

"Doc Lannon was an excellent Ranger and medic. If he said something was done you could count on it. He distinguished himself the first day in Grenada by acting both as an infantryman and as a medic. He took care of wounded Rangers and wounded Cubans alike."

Two days later, on October 27, Doc Lannon volunteered for an airmobile assault on the Cuban-held Calivigny Barracks. As the helicopter approached the landing zone, it was struck by enemy ground fire and crashed, taking the lives of SGT Lannon, SGT Stephen Slater, and SPC Philip Grenier.

Rangers Lead The Way. Rest in peace, Doc. 🇺🇸

In November 1950, Lieutenant Colonel Don Carlos Faith Jr. commanded the 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, near the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea. Chinese forces had encircled the Americans in brutal winter cold — temperatures plunging, weapons jamming in the freeze, wounded men fighting simply to survive.

Faith refused to stay behind the lines. Again and again he exposed himself to enemy fire, directing his men and personally leading counterattacks. When his battered force linked up with another surrounded American unit, he took command of the combined group — the force history remembers as Task Force Faith — and led the desperate fight to break out toward friendly lines, roadblock after roadblock standing in the way.

On April 17, 2013, Don Faith was laid to rest with full military honors at Arlington National Cemetery. His daughter was there. He had spent his last days fighting to bring his soldiers home — and more than six decades later, his country finally brought him home.

When Commander James Stockdale's A-4 Skyhawk was shot down over North Vietnam on September 9, 1965, he became the highest-ranking American naval officer in captivity — and the leader of the prisoner resistance. From inside Hoa Lo Prison, Stockdale built an organization out of whispers and wall-taps: a code of conduct for men under torture, secret communications between cells, and one unbreakable rule — nobody cooperates, nobody bows, everybody comes home with honor.

The North Vietnamese isolated him for it: years in solitary, long stretches in leg irons in the punishment annex the POWs called Alcatraz. In 1969, chosen to be paraded in a propaganda film, Stockdale beat his own face with a stool and cut himself with a razor fragment rather than be used — he would be photographed battered or not at all. His captors understood the message: this man would die before he bent. In the aftermath, the worst of the torture campaign eased.

Stockdale came home in February 1973, pictured here descending from the aircraft a free man, and received the Medal of Honor in 1976. Eight years a prisoner, four of them in solitary — and the men he led credit his iron example with bringing them home alive, together, and unashamed. He died in 2005, an admiral, a philosopher of endurance, and the standard by which American POWs are still measured.

Commander Jeremiah Denton, a Navy A-6 Intruder pilot, was shot down over North Vietnam on July 18, 1965, and dragged into the prison system the Americans called the Hanoi Hilton. American intelligence officers studying the film caught it — the first proof the world had that American POWs were being tortured. Denton endured seven years and seven months of captivity, much of it in solitary and in the punishment camp the prisoners called Alcatraz, and came home in February 1973 — the first man off the plane at Clark Air Base, where he spoke for all of them: "We are honored to have had the opportunity to serve our country under difficult circumstances." In a historic ruling, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit struck down core provisions of the 1958 Federal Switchblade Act, holding that automatically opening knives qualify as protected "Arms" under the plain text of the Second Amendment.

The appellate panel found that the federal government failed to demonstrate any historical tradition justifying an interstate commercial ban.

Louis Zamperini was an Olympic runner from California who raced at the 1936 Berlin Games, and when war came he became a bombardier on a B-24 over the Pacific. On May 27, 1943, his crippled bomber, the Green Hornet, fell into the ocean during a rescue search. Zamperini and two crewmates survived on a tiny raft — drinking rain, catching fish and birds, fending off sharks — for 47 days, among the longest sea survivals in history. One of the three died on the raft. The other two washed up alive — straight into Japanese hands.

What followed was worse than the ocean: more than two years in prisoner-of-war camps, singled out for torment by a sadistic guard the prisoners called "the Bird," who beat the famous Olympian with a belt, starved him, and tried to break the thing in him that would not bend. It never broke. Zamperini came home in 1945 carrying nightmares that nearly destroyed him with drink — until, by his own account, faith put him back together, and the man who had every reason to hate flew back to Japan to forgive his captors face to face.

He died in 2014 at 97, a torch-bearer, a mentor to generations of young men, and the subject of the book and film "Unbroken." The title is not poetry. It is a description.

On a little hill in Pennsylvania, a professor gave an order that saved the Union — and his little brother stood beside him. 🇺🇸

Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, pictured here, was a Bowdoin College professor of rhetoric who spoke ten languages and had no military training when he talked his way into the Army. What Joshua did next is studied in war colleges to this day: he fixed bayonets and ordered a downhill charge — the line swinging like a gate — that swept the stunned Confederates off the hill and, many historians believe, saved the Army of the Potomac. Thomas did not live to see the peace — disease, the silent k*ller of every Civil War camp, claimed him in 1864. Joshua carried his brother's memory through fifty more years: governor, college president, and the old soldier whose name still means Little Round Top.

Alben and Gunda Borgstrom, a farming couple from Thatcher, Utah, sent their sons to war one after another. In 1944, the telegrams began to arrive — and they did not stop.

First came word of Clyde, a Marine on Guadalcanal, lost in March 1944. Then LeRoy, a soldier, gone in the fighting in the summer of 1944. Then Rolon, lost in France. Then Rulon, an airman, missing over Europe and declared d*ad. Four brothers, lost within six months — in the Pacific and in Europe, on the sea of war's every front — while their parents kept the farm and their faith and waited for news of the boys who remained.

What was left of the family's strength, the military itself moved to protect: their fifth serving son, Boyd, was ordered home out of harm's way, released from further combat service so the Borgstrom line would not be extinguished entirely — one of the cases that hardened America's resolve to protect sole surviving sons.

In June 1948, the Army brought the four brothers home together. Thousands gathered in Utah as Clyde, LeRoy, Rolon and Rulon were laid to rest side by side in the Thatcher cemetery — four white markers, one unbearable row, and a nation's debt written in a single family's names.

FORT BENNING, Ga. (USASOC News Service, Dec. 2, 2009) -- A squad leader with the 75th Ranger Regiment was awarded the Silver Star for risking his life to save two fellow Rangers in Afghanistan.

"Any Ranger would have done the same thing," said Staff Sgt. Michael E. Norton of Alpha Company, 3rd Battalion, 75th Rangers. "The Ranger Creed says, 'I will never leave a fallen comrade.' There was no moment of thinking about what to do. I had to get my brothers, and the most important thing in my mind was how hurt they were."

Norton led his squad on an objective, Aug. 4-5, to raid an enemy combatant's headquarters camp in the mountains of northwestern Khowst Province in Afghanistan.

While moving to the objective, Norton and one of his team leaders were alerted to possible enemy combatants along the route and moved forward to assess the situation. As Norton and his team leader were attempting to identify the possible enemy in the valley, a seven—to nine-man enemy element initiated a complex, near ambush on Norton's squad from the high ground with rocket-propelled grenades and small arms fire from a position 25 meters to the squad's front.
"The fire came from our 12 o'clock and then maybe a couple of seconds later from our right and left," Norton said.

Behind the first enemy rocket-propelled grenade team, a medium machine gun on elevated ground to the northwest engaged them with highly effective fire. Two more enemy combatants were on the slope of the valley to the west, engaged the Ranger squad with an AK-47 and rocket-propelled grenades along the long axis of their formation, while another group of enemy fighters were on elevated terrain to the east, raked them with small arms fire from the rear of the Ranger squad formation.

The multiple enemy positions had effectively enveloped Norton's squad from multiple directions at a distance of 25 to 50 meters, leaving Norton and his element pinned to the floor of the valley by the intense and accurate small arms fire.

The valley left no room for maneuver; Norton, his squad and the machine gun team element behind them immediately returned fire, but they were unable to gain fire superiority over the well-established enemy.

After the second rocket-propelled grenades knocked two of his Rangers temporarily unconscious and blasted the rest of his squad with shrapnel and debris and realizing his element could not gain fire superiority, Norton shouted for his squad to break contact.

When Norton realized that two Rangers had not gotten up and were still exposed to the heavy volume of enemy fire from the high ground to the east and west, and with complete disregard for his own safety, Norton turned around and with marked distinction, purposefully charged back into the interlocking fire of the enemy ambush kill zone in order to recover his downed Rangers.

"The example of personal courage that Staff Sergeant Norton showed, to get his men out of the kill zone is a testament to his character," said Maj. Keith Carter, A Company commander. "NCOs such as Staff Sergeant Norton are the reason I wanted to serve in the 75th Ranger Regiment, and it is an honor to lead them."

Without hesitation, Norton dove down into the midst of enemy fire with his unconscious comrades, uncertain of their status.

"There was nothing fancy going on in my head besides hoping they weren't dead," said Norton.

While the rest of the element attempted to suppress the enemy, and lying next to the Rangers, Norton "started shaking and yelling as quietly as I could."

After reviving his Rangers, Norton led them back to cover through the hail of direct fire and rocket-propelled grenade strikes, saving their lives and bringing his entire squad out of the enemy onslaught intact.

"I'm proud of the actions of my squad, because we continued the mission after that," said Norton. "It was just two minutes out of our overall mission."

As his platoon fought off the enemy ambush with direct fire, mortars and close air support, Norton quickly assessed his casualties and reorganized his squad to return to the fight.

Norton continued leading his squad in the follow-on assaults through two more direct fire contacts, killing two enemy combatants.

"We receive a lot of great training here at 3rd Ranger Battalion and I was just acting on instinct," said Norton.

The training conducted by Rangers means everything on the battlefield.

"The goal of the company and battalion is to create the most realistic scenarios possible while minimizing risk," Carter said. We constantly integrate new enemy tactics from overseas into our training so that we are ready in any situation."

The overall assault force killed 20 enemy fighters and destroyed two enemy anti-aircraft guns and several other weapons, explosives, and military supplies on the objective, disrupting a major enemy headquarters and encampment.

Norton joined the Army from his hometown of Pensacola, Fla., June 2004, after graduating from West Highland Christian Academy, and has deployed six times in support of operations Enduring and Iraqi Freedom. He is the son of Jimmy and Deborah Norton of Holly, Mich.

In the spring of 1942, with America reeling from defeats, Major William Orlando Darby — just 31 years old — was given a mission: create an American unit modeled on the legendary British Commandos. That November, Rangers spearheaded the landings in North Africa, paddling ashore in darkness to silence the guns of Arzew. They fought through Sicily and Italy, at Gela and Salerno and Anzio — and at Cisterna, in January 1944, the 1st and 3rd Ranger Battalions walked into an ambush and were nearly annihilated: of 767 men who went in, only six came back.

Darby refused a safe job in Washington and returned to his men in Italy. On April 30, 1945, days before the war in Europe ended, a shell fragment took his life; he was promoted to Brigadier General on the day of his death. Today's Rangers still carry his name, his scroll, and his challenge — Darby's challenge — to lead the way. Rangers Lead The Way.

On this day, 84 years ago, October 27, 1942, 42-year-old Temporary Lieutenant-Colonel Victor Buller Turner commanded the 2nd Battalion, The Rifle Brigade at a position designated Outpost Snipe during the Second Battle of El Alamein.

His battalion had navigated through enemy minefields overnight to occupy a shallow desert depression near Kidney Ridge, only to find themselves completely isolated at daybreak.

Turner came from a family with a distinct military heritage.

His older brother, Second Lieutenant Alexander Buller Turner, had received a posthumous Victoria Cross in 1915 during the First World War, making them one of only four pairs of brothers in history to win Britain's highest military honor.

He was also related to General Sir Redvers Buller, who earned the Victoria Cross during the Anglo-Zulu War in 1879.

At Outpost Snipe, Turner's force of roughly 300 men with nineteen 6-pounder anti-tank guns faced armored elements of the German 15th and 21st Panzer Divisions and the Italian Ariete Armoured Division.

Axis forces surrounded the position and launched relentless armored counter-attacks with over ninety tanks and self-propelled guns throughout the day.

The desert heat topped 100 degrees Fahrenheit as continuous artillery, mortar, and machine-gun fire rained down into the shallow depression.

Turner moved constantly between his forward anti-tank gun pits on foot to direct fire and keep his men organized under direct shellfire.

Targeting German Panzer III and IV tanks, the gun crews held their fire until enemy armor closed within 100 yards to ensure maximum penetration.

As casualties mounted, several 6-pounder anti-tank guns were left unmanned or severely shorthanded.

When one vital gun pit was stripped of its crew except for an officer and a sergeant, Turner ran across open, bullet-swept ground to join them.

He immediately stepped into the role of loader, hauling heavy 6-pounder solid-shot shells and jamming them into the breech.

Exposed from the waist up to direct machine-gun and tank cannon fire, Turner loaded round after round as the crew engaged German armor at point-blank range.

Together, this single gun crew destroyed five German tanks at a distance of less than 50 yards before the attack stalled.

While carrying ammunition shells to keep the gun operational, a high-explosive shell burst nearby, spraying shrapnel into Turner's head.

The fragment inflicted a severe scalp wound that bled heavily down his face and neck.

Turner refused medical evacuation, brushed off aid, and remained on his feet at the forward perimeter to direct the remaining guns.

By the time the battle ended, Turner's battalion had destroyed or disabled 37 enemy tanks and self-propelled guns, shattering the Axis armored counter-offensive.

King George VI presented Turner with the Victoria Cross at Buckingham Palace on July 27, 1943.

After the war, Turner remained in the British Army and retired with the rank of Lieutenant-Colonel.

He was later appointed to the Royal Household as a Yeoman of the Guard in 1950.

In 1966, he was made a Commander of the Royal Victorian Order, and in 1967 he became Lieutenant of the Queen's Bodyguard of the Yeomen of the Guard.

Victor Buller Turner died on August 7, 1972, at the age of 72 in Ditchingham, Norfolk, and his Victoria Cross is currently displayed at the Royal Green Jackets Museum in Winchester.

The Force was disbanded in December 1944, its ranks shattered by casualties — but both nations' special forces trace their bloodline to it. They marched a thousand miles through jungle, fought an empire, and dissolved almost to the last man. 🇺🇸

In February 1944, some 3,000 American volunteers — jungle fighters, muleskinners, and men who spoke languages of the Pacific — slipped behind Japanese lines in Burma. Officially they were the 5307th Composite Unit. History knows them by their commander, Brigadier General Frank Merrill: Merrill's Marauders.

With only what they and their mules could carry, they marched farther than any American unit of the war — some 750 to 1,000 miles of mountain and jungle — and fought five major battles and dozens of skirmishes, cutting the supply lines of an army that outnumbered them many times over. Their true enemies were as much malaria, dysentery, and scrub typhus as the Japanese: men fought with fevers of 104 degrees, and the wounded who could walk were sent back to the line.

When the airfield at Myitkyina finally fell in August 1944, of the nearly 3,000 who had marched in, only about 200 remained fit for duty. Every Marauder received the Bronze Star, and in 2020 Congress awarded the unit its Gold Medal. Their legacy marches on today in the 75th Ranger Regiment, which carries the Marauders' lineage — and their impossible standard.

Their tanks were rubber. Their guns were dummies. And they saved thousands of lives. Meet the Ghost Army. 🇺🇸

In the summer of 1944, a strange unit landed in France: the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops — 1,100 men recruited not for their shooting, but for their sketchbooks. They were art students, designers, actors, architects and sound engineers, and their mission was pure deception: to impersonate entire American divisions — 30,000 men — with inflatable tanks, dummy aircraft, giant speakers blasting recorded sounds of armies on the move, and fake radio traffic.

Again and again, the Ghost Army set up its theater near the front while the real divisions slipped away to attack somewhere else. German reconnaissance saw the "tanks," heard the "army," and aimed at ghosts. Historians credit the unit with saving between 15,000 and 30,000 American lives — and then the whole story was classified for half a century. The artists never got their parade.

That finally changed on March 21, 2024, when the surviving Ghost Army veterans — most near a hundred years old — received the Congressional Gold Medal in Washington. One of their inflatable Sherman tanks, like the one pictured here, survives today in a museum: a balloon that helped win a war.

Remembering the legendary courage, fierce defiance, and ultimate sacrifice of Commander Ernest E. Evans and the crew of the USS Johnston (DD-557) during the Battle off Samar.

Outgunned by enemy battleships whose individual gun turrets weighed more than the entire Johnston, the destroyer launched a fierce torpedo attack that crippled a heavy cruiser, dodging thousands of tons of incoming armor-piercing shells. Though battered to a standstill, stripped of power, and severely damaged with half her crew wounded or killed, the Johnston kept firing until her guns jammed, with Commander Evans manually operating a gun mount himself.

ON THIS DAY — October 31, 1941: America loses its first warship of World War II — before the war even begins. 🇺🇸

In the autumn of 1941, the United States was officially at peace — but in the North Atlantic, its Navy was already fighting. American destroyers escorted convoys of supplies to Britain through waters prowled by German U-boats, and everyone knew the shooting war at sea had quietly started.

In the early hours of October 31, 1941, the destroyer USS Reuben James (DD-245), an aging four-stack ship escorting convoy HX-156, moved to shield the merchant ships from a suspected submarine. The U-552 fired first. A torpedo struck the Reuben James at her forward magazine, and the little destroyer broke in two and sank in under five minutes. Of her crew, 115 men were lost; only 44 survived — not one officer among them.

The Reuben James was the first United States Navy warship sunk in the Second World War — five weeks before Pearl Harbor — and her loss shook the nation so deeply it became a famous folk song by Woody Guthrie. On this day in 1941, 115 American sailors became the first of more than 400,000 who would not come home from that war.

ON THIS DAY — October 30, 1961: the biggest explosion in human history. 🇺🇸

At the height of the Cold War, the Soviet Union built a bomb so large it was almost a stunt: the Tsar Bomba, a hydrogen bomb designed for 100 megatons — more than 3,000 times the power of the bomb that destroyed Hiroshima — and deliberately halved to about 50 megatons so its own bomber might survive dropping it.

On October 30, 1961, over the frozen test range at Novaya Zemlya in the Arctic, a Tu-95 bomber released it by parachute and dove away at full throttle. The fireball rose miles into the sky and was seen more than 600 miles away. Windows shattered in Finland and Norway. The shockwave circled the entire Earth three times, and the mushroom cloud punched into the stratosphere.

The blast convinced the world it had seen the edge of madness: within two years, the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union signed the treaty banning atmospheric nuclear tests. The Tsar Bomba was never a practical weapon. It was a message — and on this day in 1961, the whole planet heard it.

ON THIS DAY — October 29, 1969: "LO." The first words of the internet. 🇺🇸

The internet was born as a military project. The Pentagon's Advanced Research Projects Agency — ARPA — wanted its research computers across America to talk to each other, so it built a network called ARPANET, with special router machines called Interface Message Processors.

On the night of October 29, 1969, a student programmer at UCLA named Charley Kline sat at a terminal and attempted the first host-to-host login to a computer at Stanford Research Institute, 350 miles away. He typed L — it arrived. He typed O — it arrived. He typed G — and the system crashed. The first message ever sent across what became the internet was "LO," as in "lo and behold."

Within a few years, this Cold War experiment was carrying the military's and universities' data. Within a generation, it had become the internet — the network beneath the phone in your pocket began with two letters, a crash, and a Pentagon idea on this day in 1969.

ON THIS DAY — October 28, 1942: the impossible road is finished. 🇺🇸

When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Alaska was almost unreachable — no road connected it to the rest of America, and Japanese forces soon occupied Aleutian islands. The Army's answer sounded insane: carve a 1,500-mile military highway through unmapped Canadian wilderness, muskeg, mountains and permafrost, before winter.

More than ten thousand soldiers did it — and a third of them were African American engineer regiments, men the Army had largely sidelined to labor duty, working in the worst conditions with the worst equipment, in cold that froze machinery and men alike. They felled forests, bridged wild rivers like the Peace, and laid road at a pace no one believed possible.

On October 28, 1942 — just eight months after the first bulldozer rolled — the Alaska Highway was completed, and soldiers from north and south met and shook hands on the finished road. It still carries travelers today, a monument built by hands America almost refused to use.

ON THIS DAY — October 27, 1954: the Tuskegee commander pins on a general's star. 🇺🇸

Benjamin O. Davis Jr. was the son of the Army's first Black general — and a West Point cadet who endured four years of the "silent treatment," shunned by classmates who would not speak to him, in the hope he would quit. He graduated anyway, and when America finally let Black men fly, Davis took command of the Tuskegee Airmen — the 99th Fighter Squadron and then the 332nd Fighter Group, whose Red Tails guarded bombers over Europe and built one of the finest escort records of the war.

His reward for excellence, in a segregated Air Force, was to keep proving himself for another decade. Then, on October 27, 1954, the United States Air Force promoted Benjamin O. Davis Jr. to Brigadier General — the first African American general in the service's history.

He retired a Lieutenant General, and in 1998 President Bill Clinton advanced him to full four-star General. The cadet they tried to silence with silence outlasted them all.

On May 2, 1968, Captain James E. Livingston led Echo Company, 2nd Battalion, 4th Marines, in an assault on the fortified village of Dai Do in Vietnam's Quang Tri Province — one of the fiercest fights of the war.

Livingston charged at the head of his men from bunker to bunker. Wounded in the leg, he refused medical aid and kept attacking. When a sister company was pinned down and surrounded, he led a rescue force across open ground under murderous fire, was wounded a second and then a third time — and still refused evacuation until he had personally made sure every one of his wounded Marines was carried out first. Only then did he allow himself to be taken to the rear, collapsing from loss of blood.

President Richard Nixon presented him the Medal of Honor on May 14, 1970. James Livingston served more than thirty years, retiring as a Major General — and the Marines of Dai Do never forgot the captain who would not leave the field while a single one of his men remained on it.

After nearly 28 years of service in the U.S. Army, Brigadier General Terence John Hildner was serving in Afghanistan when his life ended unexpectedly. On February 3, 2012, the 49-year-old commander of the 13th Sustainment Command (Expeditionary) was found deceased in his quarters in Kabul. Officials said he appeared to have died of natural causes, not in combat. At the time, he was the highest-ranking American service member reported to have died during the Afghanistan War.

Born in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1962, Hildner grew up in a military family, moving between places including Japan, Italy, and Colorado. He graduated from the University of Notre Dame in 1984 and began his Army career as a commissioned officer.

His early assignments included service with the 3rd Armored Cavalry Regiment at Fort Bliss and the 2nd Armored Cavalry Regiment in West Germany. He commanded a cavalry troop and took part in the final American patrol along the East-West German border before reunification.

When Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, Hildner and his troop deployed with the U.S. VII Corps during Operation Desert Storm. He later moved into Army logistics, taking on the vital work of making sure troops had the supplies, equipment, and support needed to carry out their missions.

In 2003, he led the Special Troops Battalion of the 13th Corps Support Command at Fort Hood. The unit deployed to Iraq, supporting U.S. forces near Joint Base Balad and Abu Ghraib, and later assisted with relief operations after Hurricane Katrina. From 2007 to 2009, he commanded the 23rd Quartermaster Brigade at Fort Lee, which trained more than 20,000 soldiers each year.

In 2010, Hildner assumed command of the 13th Sustainment Command (Expeditionary). The following year, he deployed to Afghanistan as deputy commander for support operations with NATO Training Mission–Afghanistan. His work included helping Afghan leaders build systems to supply and maintain their security forces.

His death in Kabul brought profound grief to his family and the soldiers who served with him. His father, Robert, told The Washington Post that he believed Terence may have suffered a heart attack; this was a family member’s belief, not a confirmed medical finding. Army accounts described the death as due to natural causes. No enemy attack or combat injury was reported.

Hildner was survived by his wife, Cindy, their four children, his parents, and his siblings. His father remembered him for his humor, determination, and analytical mind. On February 29, 2012, he was laid to rest with military honors at Arlington National Cemetery.

His decorations included the Legion of Merit, two Bronze Star Medals, the Defense Meritorious Service Medal, and the Combat Action Badge—honors earned over a career that spanned multiple conflicts and senior leadership roles.

His story is a reminder that service members can be lost overseas not only in combat, but also to illness and other non-combat circumstances. Brigadier General Terence John Hildner was a husband, father, son, and dedicated Army officer whose service ended far from home.

Rest peacefully, General Hildner. Your commitment to your soldiers and family will not be forgotten.

SOCOM is pushing for a radically lighter 10-lb 5.56mm light machine gun to supercharge operator mobility.

U.S. Special Operations Command is driving a hard modernization effort to replace the legacy Mk 46 light machine gun with an entirely new weapon system known as the Flyweight Assault Machine Gun (FAMG).

When command operators are moving fast across unforgiving terrain on direct-action raids, every single ounce counts. Traditional squad automatic weapons provide immense sustained firepower, but the physical weight of hauling a heavy gun and hundreds of rounds of linked ammunition can severely slow down a dismounted element.

SOCOM's strict requirements outline a weapon with a target weight of just 10 pounds (and no more than 11.5 pounds with its standard rail interface, bipod, and carry handle), drastically cutting down the load carried by front-line commandos.

Chambered in standard 5.56x45mm NATO, the new belt-fed machine gun is engineered to feature a maximum length of 39 inches, a side-folding collapsible stock, and a quick-change barrel that can be swapped out in under 30 seconds.

 With prototype testing and development moving forward under the U.S. Navy's NSWC Crane, SOCOM plans to award a production contract and begin fielding the new weapon to operators by fiscal year 2028.

How U.S. Marine Kyle Carpenter stared death in the face, threw himself on a grenade, and lived to earn the Medal of Honor.

On November 21, 2010, Lance Corporal Kyle Carpenter and a fellow Marine were manning a rooftop security post in the volatile Helmand Province of Afghanistan. Stationed in a small village to disrupt enemy activity and protect local residents, they suddenly found themselves targeted in a daylight Taliban attack. Without warning, an enemy hand grenade was hurled directly into their sandbagged position.

What happened next was an act of raw, instinctual selflessness that defies human logic. Without a second thought and with complete disregard for his own safety, Carpenter lunged forward and threw his body directly over the live explosive to shield his best friend from the blast.

When the grenade detonated, Carpenter absorbed the devastating brunt of the shrapnel and concussive force. The injuries were catastrophic: his right arm was shattered, his jaw was broken, he lost his right eye, and medical personnel initially flatlined him three times as he fought for his life. He endured a five-week coma, brain surgery, and nearly 40 grueling surgeries over nearly three years of intense rehabilitation.

Against all medical odds, Carpenter survived. In 2014, he received the Medal of Honor from President Barack Obama, becoming the youngest living recipient of the nation's highest military decoration. Since his medical retirement, he has gone on to run marathons, write a book, and inspire millions by turning his scars into a testament of resilience.
